analysis.title: Diversify, don't retreat
key_insights: UBS CIO moves its view on global equities to Neutral. It describes this as greater market vulnerability to earnings disappointments, not a forecast of a sell-off.

UBS also moves US equities, Asian equities excluding Japan, and emerging market equities to Neutral. It says the weight of AI, semiconductors, memory chips and technology hardware is excessive, though earnings remain high.
Concentration raises the impact of disappointments: the ten biggest companies are roughly 40% of the S&P 500, so revisions to their earnings estimates have an outsized effect on the index.
UBS expects global AI investment to rise from USD 1 trillion this year to USD 1.4 trillion next year. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and SpaceX account for roughly 80% of the total.
Funding the AI buildout requires bond issuance, where competition has intensified and borrowing has become more expensive.
Tactical preference is the Eurozone, which is less exposed to AI. UBS expects 15% earnings growth in 2027, in line with the US, from lower starting valuations.
Within industrials, UBS sees defense, automation and electrification supporting corporate performance. Health care should benefit from the longevity theme.

Public debt in developed economies is approaching levels rarely seen outside wartime. Long-term yields in the US, Japan and France are at multi-decade highs, but absolute levels and market access do not signal imminent systemic stress.

Easing inflation should support a modest decline in yields. Short-term bonds offer income and stability, 5-10 year bonds can deliver capital gains if yields fall, and some long-term government bonds look appealing at multi-decade yields.
Bonds can cushion portfolios against a sharp slowdown in AI investment, a scenario that would favor more accommodative monetary policy and lower yields.
Gold is a hedge against monetary risks, with strong demand from central banks and China. UBS prefers a strategic allocation, but says current prices may make a case for adding.
Copper is supported by investment in power grids, data centers and electrification. Supply is slow to expand because new mines take years, while demand is growing rapidly and could deepen shortages.

risk_factors: Earnings that fall short of expectations in a concentrated market.
A sharp slowdown in AI investment.
Rising interest costs on public debt and strain on public finances from aging populations and higher pension and defense spending.
Geopolitical shocks via energy prices, trade flows and interest rates.
Tighter bond market competition raising borrowing costs for AI funding.
vol_and_positioning: Concentration in the ten largest companies, about 40% of the S&P 500, magnifies the impact of earnings disappointments.
Geopolitical risks and fiscal uncertainty can drive short-term swings in bond prices.
geopolitical: Conflict in the Middle East, added to the war in Ukraine and rivalry among major powers.
US-China competition extends beyond trade to technology, critical minerals and cybersecurity.
Geopolitical shocks have passed into markets through energy prices, trade flows and interest rates.
Diplomacy could help stabilize the energy sector.
